45463: The last OT prophet promised that Elijah would come back before the Lord arrived. John the Baptist dressed like Elijah, preached like Elijah and stood up to a king like Elijah. Jesus said: he is the Elijah you were waiting for.
45464: This does not support reincarnation; Luke 1:17 speaks of 'the spirit and power of Elijah'. Some traditions also expect Elijah to return personally before the end (Rev 11 is sometimes read this way); that is a separate, debated question.
45466: Six towns were set apart where someone who killed another person by accident could flee from the avenger of blood. Inside, they were safe; they could go home freely after the death of the high priest.
45468: Hebrews speaks of believers as those who 'have fled for refuge' to lay hold of the hope set before them, an anchor that reaches behind the curtain where Jesus has entered as high priest.
45470: No condemnation for those in Christ
45471: Freedom through the death of our high priest
45472: The way to Christ made plain
45473: The cities protected the unintentional killer only; a deliberate murderer was handed over. The gospel offers refuge to the guilty, not only to the accidental offender. Hebrews' 'fled for refuge' may be an echo, but it does not name the cities.
45475: Read the high priest's death that frees the refugee as a figure of Christ's death that frees sinners.
45476: Israel had safe towns where someone who had killed a person by accident could run and be protected. Christians have seen in them a picture of running to Christ for safety. The death of the high priest set the refugee free, which many find a striking echo of Jesus.
45477: Traditional, not explicit. The detail about clear roads and signposts comes from the Mishnah (tractate Makkot), not the OT. The fit is imperfect, since the refuge was for the innocent-but-liable, not for the wicked.
45478: The temple, Christ's body and the church
45480: The temple in Jerusalem is the place where God puts his name and his glory dwells, where sacrifice is offered and prayer is heard. The prophets see its glory leave before the exile and promise a greater glory in a future house.
45481: Jesus' body, the church, and the new Jerusalem
45482: Jesus speaks of destroying 'this temple' and raising it in three days, meaning his body. Paul calls the church and the believer's body God's temple, built on Christ the cornerstone. In the new Jerusalem there is no temple, for God and the Lamb are its temple.
45483: God's fullness dwells bodily in Christ
45485: Body destroyed and raised in three days
45486: Whole new creation filled with God's presence
45487: The temple could be defiled, destroyed and abandoned by the glory; the NT presents the risen Christ as a temple that cannot be destroyed again. The temple was made with hands; the new one is 'not made with hands' (Mark 14:58).
45488: Read John 2 as a picture of the whole body of Christ, the church, destroyed and raised.
45489: Read the building of the temple as the building up of the church out of living stones from all nations.
45490: The temple was the place where heaven and earth met. The NT says that meeting place is now Jesus himself, and through him his people, and in the end the whole renewed world, where God lives with his people without any wall.
45491: Christians disagree about whether a future rebuilt temple in Jerusalem has a role in prophecy; dispensationalists often say yes, many others say the typology means the physical temple's role is fulfilled. See /debates/israel-and-church and /debates/millennium.
45492: Jacob's ladder and the Son of Man
45494: Fleeing from Esau, Jacob dreams of a stairway set on the earth reaching to heaven, with God's angels going up and down on it. He wakes and says this is the house of God and the gate of heaven.
45495: Jesus, the link between heaven and earth
45496: Jesus tells Nathanael, an 'Israelite in whom is no deceit', that he will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.
45497: The Son of Man joins earth and heaven
45498: Angels going up and down on the Son of Man
45500: Promised to Nathanael, an Israelite without deceit
45501: Jacob's ladder was a dream vision; Jesus is a person. The ladder simply stood there; Jesus is mediator by his own life and death.
45502: Read the angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man as preachers lifting up Christ the head in heaven and coming down to Christ's body on earth.
45503: Jacob dreamed of a stairway between heaven and earth. Jesus told his first disciples: you will see that I am that stairway. He is the way God comes down to us and we come up to God.
45504: Later devotional readings that turn each rung into a stage of spiritual progress (as in some monastic writings) are a separate tradition and not part of John's meaning.
45505: The sacrificial system and the one sacrifice
45507: Leviticus sets out burnt, grain, peace, sin and guilt offerings. Blood is given 'to make atonement for your souls'. Yet the prophets and psalms also say God does not ultimately desire animal sacrifice but an obedient heart.
45508: Hebrews says the law has only a shadow of the good things to come. Animal blood cannot take away sins; Christ, coming to do God's will, offered his own body once for all and sat down.
45512: Christ sat down: the work is finished
45514: Hebrews says the old sacrifices could never perfect the conscience; they served as a reminder of sin. Christ's offering was a person freely doing God's will, which Psalm 40 already hinted was what God truly wanted.
45515: Summed up the relation of the Testaments in a famous saying, often paraphrased: the New lies hidden in the Old, and the Old is made plain in the New. He applied this to the sacrifices as signs of the one true sacrifice.
45516: Defined a visible sacrifice as the sacrament, or sacred sign, of an invisible sacrifice, and said all the old sacrifices signified the one sacrifice of Christ.
45517: Israel's worship was full of sacrifices. Hebrews says they were like shadows cast ahead of a person who was coming. The shadow had the right shape, but it was not the real thing. When Christ came and gave himself, the shadow had done its job.
45518: Christians agree Christ's sacrifice fulfils the system, but differ on how the eucharist relates to it (a re-presentation of the one sacrifice in Catholic and Orthodox teaching; a memorial or spiritual feeding in most Protestant teaching). Not every detail of each offering needs a Christological meaning.
45519: Circumcision, the circumcised heart and baptism
45521: Circumcision is the sign of God's covenant with Abraham's household, given to boys on the eighth day. Already in the OT, Moses and the prophets call for a circumcised heart, and Deuteronomy promises God will circumcise his people's hearts.
45522: Circumcision of the heart by Christ
45523: Paul says believers have been circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by the putting off of the body of the flesh, the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism. True circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit.
45526: Done 'without hands' by Christ and the Spirit
45527: New creation on the 'eighth day' of resurrection (traditional)
45528: Circumcision was given to males of Abraham's household; baptism is given to men and women alike (Gal 3:27-28). Paul insists outward circumcision without the heart is worthless, so the true antitype is inward change, with baptism as its sign.
45529: Argued Christians have received a spiritual circumcision through baptism, which Enoch and others had without fleshly circumcision.
45530: Used the eighth-day timing of circumcision in debate about whether infants could be baptised before the eighth day; his council said they could.
45531: Circumcision marked a boy as part of God's covenant people. Even in the OT, God said what he really wanted was a 'circumcised heart'. Paul says Christ does that inner surgery, and baptism is now the outward sign of belonging.
45532: Whether Colossians 2 makes baptism the direct replacement of circumcision is central to the infant-baptism debate: paedobaptists see continuity of the covenant sign to children; credobaptists argue the antitype is the inward circumcision of believers only. See /debates/baptism.
45533: The exodus and salvation in Christ
45534: God hears Israel's cry, judges Egypt, rescues his people through the Passover and the sea, and brings them to Sinai to be his treasured possession. The prophets later promise a new and greater exodus from exile.
45536: At the transfiguration, Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about his 'departure' (Greek *exodos*) to be accomplished at Jerusalem. Believers are rescued from the domain of darkness and made a royal priesthood, the very titles given to Israel at Sinai.
45541: The exodus freed a single nation from a political oppressor; the NT speaks of freedom from sin and death for people of every nation. Israel's wilderness generation largely fell away, which Paul uses as a warning rather than a promise.
45542: Retold the whole exodus night as the outline of the gospel, with Egypt's firstborn struck and Israel kept by the lamb's blood.
45543: Read the exodus as the soul's journey out of slavery to the passions toward God.
45544: The exodus is the great rescue story of the OT. The NT tells the story of Jesus with the same shape: a lamb, a crossing through water, a journey, a people made God's own. Luke even calls Jesus' death and resurrection his 'exodus'.
45545: Liberation theologies read the exodus primarily as God's rescue of the poor and oppressed in history, while other traditions stress its spiritual fulfilment. The NT supports a spiritual reading clearly; how far the political dimension carries over is debated.
45546: The promised land and the inheritance to come
45548: God promises Abraham's descendants the land of Canaan, a good land flowing with milk and honey. Under Joshua Israel enters it and receives rest, though the hold on it is always conditional and is later lost in exile.
45549: The inheritance and the new creation
45550: Paul says Abraham was promised he would inherit 'the world'. Jesus says the meek will inherit the earth. Hebrews says the patriarchs were looking for a better, heavenly country, a city God has prepared. Revelation ends with a new heaven and new earth.
45551: The world promised to all who share Abraham's faith
45553: An inheritance kept in heaven, imperishable
45554: God dwelling with humanity in the new creation
45555: Canaan could be lost through disobedience and was entered by conquest. The NT inheritance is 'imperishable, undefiled and unfading' and global in scope.
45556: Insisted the promise of land to Abraham will be fulfilled literally in a renewed earth at the resurrection, against those who spiritualised it away.
45557: Read the land mainly as the soul's spiritual inheritance and heavenly realities, a reading Irenaeus' approach resisted.
45558: God promised Abraham a land. The NT says the promise was bigger than a strip of the Middle East: it pointed to the whole renewed earth, which all of Abraham's spiritual children will inherit.
45559: Whether the typology means the land promise to ethnic Israel is fulfilled and widened, or still awaits a specific future fulfilment, is a live debate between covenant theology, dispensationalism and others, with real political consequences today. See /debates/israel-and-church.
45560: Hagar and Sarah: Paul's allegory of two covenants
45561: Hagar and Sarah, Ishmael and Isaac
45562: Abraham has a son by Hagar the Egyptian slave woman, born in the ordinary way, and later a son by Sarah the free woman, born by God's promise in old age. Hagar and Ishmael are eventually sent away.
45564: Paul says these things may be read allegorically: the two women are two covenants. Hagar stands for Mount Sinai and the present Jerusalem, in slavery; Sarah for the Jerusalem above, which is free and is our mother. Believers are children of promise like Isaac.
45565: The covenant from Sinai, bearing children for slavery
45566: The Jerusalem above, mother of the free
45567: Trying to belong to God by human effort
45569: Those of the flesh persecute those of the Spirit
45570: Paul's reading reverses what his opponents would have expected: they would identify Jews with Sarah's line. In Genesis, God also cares for Hagar and Ishmael, sees Hagar's misery and blesses Ishmael (Gen 16:13; Gen 21:17-20), which Paul's argument does not address.
45571: Cited Galatians 4 as proof that the apostles themselves read the OT allegorically, giving licence for his wider method.
45572: Noted that Paul used the word 'allegory' loosely, meaning a type, and that the history still really happened.
45573: Paul takes the story of Abraham's two wives and two sons and uses it as a picture. One son was born from human planning, the other from God's promise. Paul says trying to be right with God through the law is like being Hagar's child; trusting God's promise makes you Sarah's child, free.
45574: This is Paul's own allegory (he uses the word *allēgoroumena*) in a heated argument against teachers urging gentiles to be circumcised. It has been misused to cast the Jewish people as 'slaves' or rejected; Paul's target is a specific teaching, and Romans 9-11 shows his ongoing hope for Israel. It is also not a licence to allegorise any story at will.
45575: Israel, God's son, and Jesus the true Israel
45577: God calls Israel 'my firstborn son' and brings him out of Egypt. In the wilderness Israel is tested for forty years and often fails. Isaiah speaks of the servant who is called 'Israel'.
45579: Matthew says Jesus' return from Egypt fulfils 'Out of Egypt I called my son'. After passing through the waters of baptism, Jesus is tested forty days in the wilderness and answers each temptation with Deuteronomy, succeeding where Israel failed.
45581: Passes through the Jordan in baptism
45582: Forty days tested in the wilderness
45585: Hosea 11:1 in context looks back on Israel's past; it is not a prediction. Matthew reads it as a pattern Jesus relives and completes. Israel was a disobedient son; Jesus is the obedient one.
45586: Discussed whether Matthew drew Hosea 11:1 from the Hebrew rather than the Greek OT (which reads 'his children'), and defended Matthew's use.
45587: Hosea was remembering the exodus when he wrote 'out of Egypt I called my son'. Matthew sees Jesus walking the same road Israel walked: out of Egypt, through the water, into the wilderness. But where Israel stumbled, Jesus stays faithful. He sums up Israel in himself.
45588: Matthew's 'fulfilled' here does not mean Hosea made a prediction; it means the pattern reaches its full meaning in Jesus. Seeing Jesus as 'true Israel' is sometimes pushed into replacement theology (the church replaces Israel); many interpreters who accept this typology reject that conclusion. See /debates/israel-and-church.
45589: The scarlet cord in Rahab's window
45590: Rahab, a Canaanite woman of Jericho, hides Israel's spies. They tell her to tie a scarlet cord in her window; everyone in her house when the city falls will be spared.
45592: The NT honours Rahab for her faith and her actions and places her in Jesus' family line. Early Christians read the scarlet cord as a sign of redemption through the blood of the Lord.
45593: Christ's blood protects those who shelter in him
45595: The NT praises Rahab's faith and hospitality but never mentions the cord. The cord was a practical signal for soldiers, not a sacrifice.
45596: Said the scarlet thread made plain that redemption would come through the blood of the Lord to all who believe and hope in God, and that Rahab showed both faith and prophecy.
45597: Made the same link between the scarlet sign and the blood of Christ.
45598: Read Rahab's house as the church, outside of which no one is saved.
45599: Rahab hung a red cord in her window and her family survived when Jericho fell. Christians very early on saw a picture of being kept safe by Christ's blood. It is a lovely image, but it comes from the early church, not from the NT.
45600: A good example of a traditional type: 1 Clement 12 (around AD 96) makes the link, but no NT writer does. It is fine as illustration, but it should not be taught as if the Bible itself said it. Origen's 'no salvation outside Rahab's house' is a further application.
